title: 205. Algebra, Equations & Inequalities: Solving Reciprocal Inequalities by Sign Analysis
description: A comprehensive mathematics curriculum progressing from foundational numeracy and core mathematical concepts to algebra, geometry, calculus, linear algebra, probability, statistics, discrete mathematics, optimization, mathematical foundations of AI, advanced pure mathematics, and emerging research methods.

questions.concept: Solving reciprocal inequalities with positive quotient
questions.learningObjective: Determine the solution of \(\frac{1}{x}>0\) by sign analysis.
questions.question: Solve \(\frac{1}{x}>0\).
questions.explanation: The fraction \(\frac{1}{x}\) has the same sign as \(x\) because the numerator \(1\) is positive. It is positive when \(x>0\). The denominator cannot be zero, so \(x\ne 0\). Therefore the solution is \(x>0\).
questions.hint: Determine where the numerator and denominator have the same sign.

questions.concept: Solving reciprocal inequalities with negative quotient
questions.question: Solve \(\frac{1}{x-2}<0\).
questions.explanation: The numerator \(1\) is positive, so the fraction is negative exactly when the denominator is negative. Thus \(x-2<0\), which gives \(x<2\). The value \(x=2\) is excluded because it makes the denominator zero.
questions.hint: The numerator is positive, so the sign of the fraction is the sign of the denominator.

questions.concept: Solving reciprocal inequalities with a constant bound
questions.learningObjective: Solve \(\frac{1}{x}\le1\) by bringing all terms to one side and using sign analysis.
questions.question: Solve \(\frac{1}{x}\le1\).
questions.explanation:
Subtract \(1\) from both sides, then combine the terms into a single fraction:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{1}{x}-1 &\le 0\\
\frac{1-x}{x} &\le 0
\end{aligned}
\]
The critical values are \(x=0\) (excluded) and \(x=1\). On \(x<0\), the numerator \(1-x>0\) and the denominator \(x<0\), so the quotient is negative and satisfies the inequality. On \(0<x<1\), both numerator and denominator are positive, so the quotient is positive. On \(x\ge1\), at \(x=1\) the quotient is \(0\), and for \(x>1\) the quotient is negative. Therefore the solution is \(x<0\) or \(x\ge1\).
questions.hint: Subtract \(1\) from both sides and combine the expression into a single fraction.

questions.concept: Solving reciprocal inequalities with a linear denominator
questions.question: Solve \(\frac{1}{x+1}\ge2\).
questions.explanation:
Subtract \(2\) from both sides, then combine the terms into a single fraction and simplify the numerator:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{1}{x+1}-2 &\ge 0\\
\frac{1-2(x+1)}{x+1} &\ge 0\\
\frac{-2x-1}{x+1} &\ge 0
\end{aligned}
\]
The critical values are \(x=-1\) (excluded) and \(x=-\frac{1}{2}\). The numerator \(-2x-1\) is nonnegative when \(x\le-\frac{1}{2}\). The denominator \(x+1\) is positive when \(x>-1\). Both conditions together give \(-1<x\le-\frac{1}{2}\). The value \(x=-1\) is not allowed.
questions.hint: Bring \(2\) to the left side and combine the expression over the common denominator.

questions.concept: Solving reciprocal inequalities with a shifted denominator
questions.question: Solve \(\frac{2}{x-1}>1\).
questions.explanation:
Subtract \(1\) from both sides, then combine the terms into a single fraction and simplify the numerator:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{2}{x-1}-1 &> 0\\
\frac{2-(x-1)}{x-1} &> 0\\
\frac{3-x}{x-1} &> 0
\end{aligned}
\]
The critical values are \(x=1\) (excluded) and \(x=3\). On \(x<1\), the numerator \(3-x\) is positive and the denominator \(x-1\) is negative, so the quotient is negative. On \(1<x<3\), both numerator and denominator are positive, so the quotient is positive. On \(x>3\), the numerator is negative and the denominator is positive, so the quotient is negative. At \(x=3\), the quotient is \(0\), which is not greater than \(0\). Therefore the solution is \(1<x<3\).
questions.hint: Subtract \(1\) and combine the expression into a single fraction.

questions.question: Solve \(\frac{1}{x+2}\le\frac{1}{x-3}\).
questions.explanation:
Bring all terms to the left, then combine them over the common denominator and simplify the numerator:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{1}{x+2}-\frac{1}{x-3} &\le 0\\
\frac{(x-3)-(x+2)}{(x+2)(x-3)} &\le 0\\
\frac{-5}{(x+2)(x-3)} &\le 0
\end{aligned}
\]
The numerator \(-5\) is negative, so the fraction is nonpositive when the denominator is positive. Thus
\[
(x+2)(x-3)>0
\]
This product is positive when \(x<-2\) or \(x>3\). The values \(x=-2\) and \(x=3\) are excluded because they make a denominator zero.
questions.hint: Combine the two fractions, then determine where the resulting quotient is nonpositive.

questions.concept: Comparing reciprocal expressions with a positive difference
questions.question: Solve \(\frac{1}{x-1}\ge\frac{1}{x+2}\).
questions.explanation:
Bring all terms to the left, then combine them over the common denominator and simplify the numerator:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{1}{x-1}-\frac{1}{x+2} &\ge 0\\
\frac{(x+2)-(x-1)}{(x-1)(x+2)} &\ge 0\\
\frac{3}{(x-1)(x+2)} &\ge 0
\end{aligned}
\]
The numerator \(3\) is positive, so the fraction is nonnegative when the denominator is positive. Thus
\[
(x-1)(x+2)>0
\]
This product is positive when \(x<-2\) or \(x>1\). The values \(x=-2\) and \(x=1\) are excluded.
questions.hint: Combine the fractions and analyze the sign of the denominator.

questions.concept: Solving reciprocal inequalities with a positive constant
questions.question: Solve \(\frac{1}{x+1}\ge\frac{1}{3}\).
questions.explanation:
Subtract \(\frac{1}{3}\) from both sides, then combine the terms over the common denominator and simplify the numerator:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{1}{x+1}-\frac{1}{3} &\ge 0\\
\frac{3-(x+1)}{3(x+1)} &\ge 0\\
\frac{2-x}{3(x+1)} &\ge 0
\end{aligned}
\]
The factor \(3\) in the denominator is positive. The critical values are \(x=-1\) (excluded) and \(x=2\) (included). On \(x<-1\), the numerator \(2-x\) is positive and the denominator \(x+1\) is negative, so the quotient is negative. On \(-1<x\le2\), the quotient is nonnegative. On \(x>2\), the quotient is negative. Therefore the solution is \(-1<x\le2\).
questions.hint: Move all terms to one side and combine over the common denominator.

questions.question: Solve \(\frac{1}{x-2}>\frac{1}{x+1}\).
questions.explanation:
Bring all terms to the left, then combine them over the common denominator and simplify the numerator:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{1}{x-2}-\frac{1}{x+1} &> 0\\
\frac{(x+1)-(x-2)}{(x-2)(x+1)} &> 0\\
\frac{3}{(x-2)(x+1)} &> 0
\end{aligned}
\]
The numerator \(3\) is positive, so the fraction is positive exactly when the denominator is positive. Thus
\[
(x-2)(x+1)>0
\]
This product is positive when \(x<-1\) or \(x>2\). The values \(x=-1\) and \(x=2\) are excluded.
questions.hint: Combine the fractions; since the numerator is positive, analyze where the denominator is positive.

questions.concept: Solving reciprocal inequalities with a constant on the right
questions.learningObjective: Solve \(\frac{1}{x-1}\le2\) by sign analysis and interval testing.
questions.question: Solve \(\frac{1}{x-1}\le2\).
questions.explanation:
Subtract \(2\) from both sides, then combine the terms into a single fraction and simplify the numerator:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{1}{x-1}-2 &\le 0\\
\frac{1-2(x-1)}{x-1} &\le 0\\
\frac{3-2x}{x-1} &\le 0
\end{aligned}
\]
The critical values are \(x=1\) (excluded) and \(x=\frac{3}{2}\) (included). On \(x<1\), the numerator \(3-2x\) is positive and the denominator \(x-1\) is negative, so the quotient is negative and satisfies the inequality. On \(1<x<\frac{3}{2}\), the quotient is positive. On \(x\ge\frac{3}{2}\), the quotient is nonpositive. Therefore the solution is \(x<1\) or \(x\ge\frac{3}{2}\).
questions.hint: Subtract \(2\) and combine into a single fraction, then test the sign on each interval.
